name: Introduction to Economics
description: An accessible introduction to fundamental economic principles covering scarcity, supply and demand, market structures, national income, and the roles of money and government in the economy.

modules.title: Scarcity & Economic Thinking
modules.objectives: Define scarcity and explain why it is the central economic problem; distinguish between wants and needs; explain opportunity cost and the role of trade-offs in economic decision-making.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e §1.1 — scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Scarcity & Economic Thinking; use with the worked data in the assignment
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 1 review questions — complete the questions tied to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Analyze these four choices using scarcity and opportunity cost: (A) spend $30 on a concert ticket or save it for a $90 course fee; (B) use two free hours for paid work at $14 per hour or exam study; (C) a town uses its final vacant lot for a park or a clinic; (D) a bakery uses its last 20 kg of flour for bread or cakes. For each, identify the scarce resource, chosen option, and next-best alternative. Submit: a four-row decision table plus a 250-word explanation. Include: one explicit opportunity-cost statement per case and one distinction between a want and a need. Evaluation: 100% total — concepts 35%, case application 35%, reasoning 20%, clarity 10%.

modules.title: Supply & Demand Basics
modules.objectives: State the law of demand and the law of supply; list the determinants of supply and demand; draw supply and demand curves and identify factors that shift each curve. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e §3.1 — demand, supply, and equilibrium
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Supply & Demand Basics; use with the worked data in the assignment
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 3 review questions — complete the questions tied to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Use this supplied weekly market schedule for reusable bottles: price $8/$10/$12/$14/$16; quantity demanded 90/80/70/60/50; quantity supplied 30/50/70/90/110. Plot both curves, identify equilibrium, and explain whether $10 creates a shortage or surplus and by how many units. Then predict the demand shift if a close substitute becomes more expensive. Submit: one labeled graph, calculations, and 200–250 words. Include: axes, units, equilibrium, disequilibrium calculation, and shift reasoning. Evaluation: 100% total — graph 30%, calculations 30%, economic reasoning 30%, clarity 10%.

modules.title: Market Equilibrium & Price
modules.objectives: Identify market equilibrium as the price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded; predict the effects of supply and demand shifts on equilibrium price and quantity; explain surpluses and shortages.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e §3.2 — shifts and new equilibria
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Market Equilibrium & Price; use with the worked data in the assignment
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 3 review questions — complete the questions tied to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Start with this equilibrium for bus passes: at $20, quantity demanded and supplied are both 1,000. A new employer subsidy increases demand at every price, while higher fuel costs reduce supply at every price. Draw the original curves and both shifts. State what can be concluded with certainty about equilibrium price and explain why the direction of equilibrium quantity depends on the relative shift sizes. Submit: before/after diagrams and a 300-word analysis. Include: both shift causes, directional reasoning, and a warning against claiming an exact price or quantity without full schedules. Evaluation: 100% total — diagram 30%, shift logic 35%, uncertainty reasoning 25%, clarity 10%.

modules.title: Elasticity
modules.objectives: Define and calculate price elasticity of demand and supply; distinguish elastic from inelastic demand; explain how elasticity affects total revenue and the impact of taxes.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e §5.1 — midpoint elasticity calculations
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Elasticity; use with the worked data in the assignment
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 5 review questions — complete the questions tied to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand between Point A (price $12, quantity 120) and Point B (price $15, quantity 84). Show the percentage change in price, percentage change in quantity, elasticity magnitude, classification, and predicted direction of total revenue. Submit: a calculation sheet plus a 150-word interpretation. Include: midpoint formulas, absolute elasticity for classification, and revenue at both points. Evaluation: 100% total — calculations 45%, classification 20%, revenue reasoning 25%, clarity 10%.

modules.title: Consumer Choice & Utility
modules.objectives: Define utility and marginal utility; apply the law of diminishing marginal utility; explain how consumers maximize utility by allocating spending across goods.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e §6.1 — utility and consumer choice
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Consumer Choice & Utility; use with the worked data in the assignment
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 6 review questions — complete the questions tied to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: A student has $12. Snacks cost $3 and drinks cost $2. Marginal utility by unit is: snacks 30, 21, 12, 6; drinks 18, 14, 10, 6, 2. Compute marginal utility per dollar for every unit and choose the bundle that maximizes total utility without exceeding $12. Submit: a completed table, chosen bundle, total spending, and 200-word justification. Include: the diminishing-marginal-utility pattern and the next rejected unit. Evaluation: 100% total — table accuracy 35%, bundle 25%, marginal reasoning 30%, clarity 10%.

modules.title: Production & Costs
modules.objectives: Distinguish fixed from variable costs and short-run from long-run production; calculate total cost, average total cost, and marginal cost; explain the relationship between production and costs.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e §7.3 — fixed, variable, average, and marginal cost
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Production & Costs; use with the worked data in the assignment
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 7 review questions — complete the questions tied to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: A fictional firm has fixed cost $120. For output 0–5 units, variable cost is $0, $40, $70, $105, $155, and $225. Calculate total cost, average fixed cost, average variable cost, average total cost, and marginal cost for each positive output level; graph ATC and MC. Submit: the completed table, graph, and 200-word explanation of where MC crosses or approaches ATC. Include: formulas and labeled units. Evaluation: 100% total — calculations 45%, graph 25%, cost reasoning 20%, clarity 10%.

modules.title: Types of Market Structures
modules.objectives: Identify and compare the four main market structures — perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, and monopoly — using characteristics such as number of sellers, product type, and barriers to entry.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e Chapter 10 introduction — compare perfect competition and monopoly with monopolistic competition and oligopoly
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Types of Market Structures; use with the worked data in the assignment
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 10 review questions — use the imperfect-competition items with the four-structure comparison in this module
modules.assignment: Classify four fictional markets: (A) hundreds of identical-grain farms with easy entry; (B) one regulated water network with high infrastructure barriers; (C) four airlines whose pricing decisions affect one another; (D) many restaurants differentiated by menu and location. Create a comparison chart covering sellers, product differentiation, entry barriers, price power, and likely structure. Submit: the chart plus a 300-word defense of all four classifications. Include: one ambiguity or limitation for a real-world classification. Evaluation: 100% total — classification 35%, criteria 30%, justification 25%, clarity 10%.

modules.title: Labor Markets
modules.objectives: Explain how wages are determined by supply and demand in labor markets; analyze the effects of minimum wage laws; describe the role of unions and human capital in wage differences.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e §14.1 — labor demand, labor supply, and wages
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Labor Markets; use with the worked data in the assignment
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 14 review questions — complete the questions tied to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Use this fictional labor-market schedule: hourly wage $12/$14/$16/$18; labor demanded 140/120/100/80 workers; labor supplied 60/80/100/120 workers. Identify equilibrium. Then impose a $18 minimum wage and calculate the labor surplus. Finally, explain how an employer-funded certification that raises worker productivity could shift labor demand. Submit: graph, calculations, and 250-word analysis. Include: equilibrium, surplus, demand-shift mechanism, and one limitation of the simplified model. Evaluation: 100% total — graph/calculations 40%, labor-market reasoning 35%, limitation 15%, clarity 10%.

quizQuestions.question: Scarcity in economics means that:
options: Resources are limited relative to unlimited wants
quizQuestions.answer: Resources are limited relative to unlimited wants
quizQuestions.explanation: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem: human wants are unlimited while the resources to satisfy them are finite, forcing individuals and societies to make choices.

quizQuestions.question: Opportunity cost is best defined as:
options: The monetary price of a good
The value of the next best alternative foregone
The cost of producing one additional unit
The total cost of all resources used
quizQuestions.answer: The value of the next best alternative foregone
quizQuestions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of what you give up when you make a choice — the best alternative you did not choose.

quizQuestions.question: A workshop can produce either 12 tables or 36 chairs per day. What is the opportunity cost of one table?
quizQuestions.answer: 3 chairs
quizQuestions.explanation: Producing 12 tables uses the capacity for 36 chairs, so each table costs 36/12 = 3 chairs.

quizQuestions.question: The law of demand states that, all else equal:
options: As price rises, quantity demanded rises
As price falls, quantity demanded falls
As price rises, quantity demanded falls
quizQuestions.answer: As price rises, quantity demanded falls
quizQuestions.explanation: The law of demand reflects the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded — consumers buy less of a good as its price increases.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following would SHIFT the demand curve for pizza to the RIGHT?
options: A decrease in the price of pizza
An increase in consumer income (pizza is a normal good)
An increase in the price of a pizza ingredient
A decrease in the number of pizza restaurants
quizQuestions.answer: An increase in consumer income (pizza is a normal good)
quizQuestions.explanation: Higher income increases demand for normal goods, shifting the demand curve right (more demanded at every price). A price change causes movement along the curve, not a shift.

quizQuestions.question: The law of supply states that, all else equal:
options: As price rises, quantity supplied falls
As price falls, quantity supplied rises
As price rises, quantity supplied rises
Supply is not affected by price
quizQuestions.answer: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
quizQuestions.explanation: Producers are willing to supply more of a good at higher prices because higher prices make production more profitable.

quizQuestions.question: If printers and ink cartridges are complements, a fall in printer prices will most likely:
options: Cause movement along the printer supply curve only
quizQuestions.answer: Shift cartridge demand right
quizQuestions.explanation: Cheaper printers increase printer purchases and therefore increase demand for the complementary cartridges.

quizQuestions.question: Market equilibrium occurs when:
options: The government sets a fair price
quizQuestions.answer: Quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
quizQuestions.explanation: Equilibrium is the price at which the market 'clears' — the amount sellers want to sell exactly equals the amount buyers want to buy.

quizQuestions.question: A surplus in a market means:
options: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the current price
quizQuestions.answer: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the current price
quizQuestions.explanation: A surplus (excess supply) occurs when the price is above equilibrium — producers want to sell more than buyers want to buy, putting downward pressure on price.

quizQuestions.question: If both supply and demand increase simultaneously, what definitely happens to equilibrium quantity?
options: It depends on the size of each shift
quizQuestions.answer: It rises
quizQuestions.explanation: Both a supply increase and a demand increase put upward pressure on quantity. Equilibrium quantity definitely rises; the effect on price is ambiguous.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: When demand increases and supply remains unchanged, equilibrium price will?
quizQuestions.answer: Rise
quizQuestions.explanation: A correct response identifies "Rise" and connects it to the module context.

quizQuestions.question: If a 10% rise in price leads to a 20% fall in quantity demanded, price elasticity of demand is:
quizQuestions.answer: 2.0 — elastic
quizQuestions.explanation: PED = % change in Qd / % change in P = 20% / 10% = 2.0. Since PED > 1, demand is elastic — consumers are very responsive to price changes.

quizQuestions.question: Goods with few substitutes tend to have:
quizQuestions.answer: Inelastic demand
quizQuestions.explanation: With few substitutes, consumers cannot easily switch away when price rises, making demand less responsive to price — inelastic demand.

quizQuestions.question: If demand is inelastic and price rises, total revenue will:
quizQuestions.answer: Increase
quizQuestions.explanation: With inelastic demand, the percentage decrease in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage price increase, so price × quantity (total revenue) rises.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following goods is likely to have the MOST elastic demand?
options: A specific luxury sports car brand
quizQuestions.answer: A specific luxury sports car brand
quizQuestions.explanation: Luxury goods with many substitutes (other car brands or models) tend to have elastic demand — a price increase causes a large drop in quantity demanded.

quizQuestions.question: In Consumer Choice & Utility, Marginal utility is the:
options: Total satisfaction from consuming a good
Additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit
Change in price per unit consumed
quizQuestions.answer: Additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit
quizQuestions.explanation: Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction (utility) gained from consuming one additional unit of a good or service.

quizQuestions.question: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that:
options: Total utility eventually decreases with consumption
Marginal utility increases as more units are consumed
As more units are consumed, each additional unit provides less additional satisfaction
quizQuestions.answer: As more units are consumed, each additional unit provides less additional satisfaction
quizQuestions.explanation: After a point, each additional unit of a good adds less to total utility than the previous unit did — the classic pattern of diminishing marginal utility.

quizQuestions.question: Good A costs $2 and has marginal utility 18; Good B costs $3 and has marginal utility 21. Which next unit gives more marginal utility per dollar?
options: Cannot be compared without total utility
quizQuestions.answer: Good A
quizQuestions.explanation: Good A yields 18/2 = 9 utility per dollar, compared with 21/3 = 7 for Good B.

quizQuestions.question: A consumer’s total utility rises from 42 to 50 when a third unit is consumed. The marginal utility of the third unit is:
quizQuestions.explanation: Marginal utility is the additional satisfaction from one more unit, so it equals the change in total utility: 50 − 42 = 8 utility units.

quizQuestions.question: In Production & Costs, Fixed costs are costs that:
options: Do not change with output in the short run
Depend on the number of workers hired
quizQuestions.answer: Do not change with output in the short run
quizQuestions.explanation: Fixed costs (rent, insurance, equipment) must be paid regardless of how much is produced; they cannot be avoided in the short run.

quizQuestions.question: In Production & Costs, Marginal cost is the:
options: Cost of producing one more unit of output
quizQuestions.answer: Cost of producing one more unit of output
quizQuestions.explanation: Marginal cost = change in total cost / change in quantity. It measures the additional cost of producing one more unit.

quizQuestions.question: If a firm has total costs of $500 at 10 units and $550 at 11 units, the marginal cost of the 11th unit is:
quizQuestions.explanation: MC = change in total cost / change in quantity = ($550 − $500) / (11 − 10) = $50.

quizQuestions.question: A firm has fixed cost $120 and produces 30 units. Its average fixed cost is:
quizQuestions.explanation: Average fixed cost equals fixed cost divided by output: $120/30 = $4 per unit.

quizQuestions.question: In the short run, which input is most likely fixed for a restaurant?
options: Size of its leased dining space
quizQuestions.answer: Size of its leased dining space
quizQuestions.explanation: A leased facility usually cannot be adjusted quickly, while labor hours and ingredients can vary with output.

quizQuestions.question: Which market structure has the MOST competition?
quizQuestions.answer: Perfect competition
quizQuestions.explanation: Perfect competition has the most competition: many sellers, identical products, free entry/exit, and perfect information — no single firm has pricing power.

quizQuestions.question: A monopoly differs from perfect competition primarily because the monopolist:
options: Is the sole seller and faces no close substitutes
Sets price equal to marginal cost
quizQuestions.answer: Is the sole seller and faces no close substitutes
quizQuestions.explanation: A monopoly is defined by a single seller with significant barriers to entry and no close substitute for its product, giving it substantial pricing power.

quizQuestions.question: Many restaurants compete locally, but each differentiates its menu and location. This market is best classified as:
options: A differentiated-seller market with open entry
quizQuestions.answer: A differentiated-seller market with open entry
quizQuestions.explanation: Many sellers, differentiated products, and relatively open entry are characteristic of monopolistic competition.

quizQuestions.question: In a competitive labor market, the equilibrium wage is determined by:
options: The intersection of labor supply and labor demand
quizQuestions.answer: The intersection of labor supply and labor demand
quizQuestions.explanation: Like any competitive market, wages in a competitive labor market are determined by supply and demand forces.

quizQuestions.question: A minimum wage set above the market equilibrium wage will most likely:
quizQuestions.answer: Decrease employment
quizQuestions.explanation: A minimum wage above equilibrium creates a surplus of labor (more workers want jobs than employers want to hire), reducing employment below the free-market level.

quizQuestions.question: In Labor Markets, Human capital refers to:
options: The knowledge and skills workers acquire through education and training
quizQuestions.answer: The knowledge and skills workers acquire through education and training
quizQuestions.explanation: Human capital is the productive capacity embodied in workers through education, on-the-job training, and experience.

quizQuestions.question: A new certification makes workers more productive. In a competitive labor market, this most directly tends to:
quizQuestions.answer: Shift labor demand right
quizQuestions.explanation: Higher productivity raises the value of marginal product and firms’ willingness to hire workers at each wage.

questions.question: Which choice best distinguishes a need from a want in an introductory scarcity analysis?
options: Basic nutrition is a need; a premium concert ticket is a want
Every expensive item is a need
Every inexpensive item is a want
Needs are unlimited but wants are fixed
questions.answer: Basic nutrition is a need; a premium concert ticket is a want
questions.explanation: Needs support basic functioning, while wants add comfort or enjoyment; both still use scarce resources and require choices.

questions.question: If the price of coffee itself falls while all other demand determinants stay constant, the market experiences:
options: An increase in quantity demanded along the existing demand curve
A rightward shift of the demand curve
A leftward shift of the supply curve
questions.answer: An increase in quantity demanded along the existing demand curve
questions.explanation: A change in a good’s own price causes movement along its demand curve; a lower price raises quantity demanded without shifting the curve.

questions.question: If demand decreases while supply increases, which equilibrium change is certain?
questions.explanation: Both a demand decrease and a supply increase push equilibrium price downward; their effects on equilibrium quantity oppose one another, so quantity is ambiguous.

questions.question: Using the given information, what is the correct result? Using the midpoint method, if price rises from $10 to $20 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80, PED =
questions.explanation: Using midpoint percentages: quantity changes by 20/90 = 22.22% and price changes by 10/15 = 66.67%; the elasticity magnitude is 22.22/66.67 ≈ 0.33, so demand is inelastic over this interval.

questions.question: Total utility is maximized at the point where:
questions.explanation: Total utility reaches its maximum when marginal utility is zero. Consuming beyond this point causes marginal utility to become negative, reducing total utility.

questions.question: A firm has fixed cost $100 and variable cost $300 when it produces 20 units. Its average total cost is:
questions.explanation: Total cost is $100 + $300 = $400. Average total cost is $400 / 20 = $20 per unit.

questions.question: Which characteristic is shared by perfect competition and monopolistic competition?
questions.explanation: Both structures have many competing sellers; monopolistic competition differs because products are differentiated.

questions.question: Which change shifts the supply curve rather than causing movement along it?
options: A change in the product's own price
A movement upward along the supply curve
A change in quantity supplied caused only by price
questions.explanation: A change in input costs changes how much firms are willing to supply at every product price, shifting the curve; a change in the product’s own price causes movement along the curve.

questions.question: Good A provides 18 marginal-utility units for $3, while Good B provides 20 for $5. Which next purchase gives more marginal utility per dollar?
options: There is not enough information to compare
questions.explanation: Good A provides 18/3 = 6 utility units per dollar, compared with 20/5 = 4 for Good B.

questions.question: Which cost is most likely fixed in the short run for a bakery?
options: Hourly pay for extra production workers
questions.explanation: Storefront rent does not vary with the number of loaves produced during the short-run rental period, unlike ingredients, packaging, or variable labor.

questions.question: If demand is elastic and price decreases, total revenue will:
questions.explanation: With elastic demand (PED > 1), a price decrease causes a proportionally larger increase in quantity demanded, raising total revenue.

questions.question: What most clearly distinguishes an oligopoly from the other major market structures?
options: Strategic interdependence among a few dominant firms
A very large number of price-taking firms
No barriers to entry and identical products
A single buyer with no sellers
questions.answer: Strategic interdependence among a few dominant firms
questions.explanation: Because a few firms dominate an oligopoly, each firm must anticipate how rivals will respond; this strategic interdependence is its defining feature.

questions.question: Which of the following would DECREASE labor demand in a particular industry?
options: An increase in demand for the industry's product
A technological innovation that replaces workers with machines
An increase in human capital investment
questions.answer: A technological innovation that replaces workers with machines
questions.explanation: Labor-saving technology reduces the quantity of labor needed to produce each unit, shifting the labor demand curve left.

questions.question: A market schedule shows: at $10, Qd=90 and Qs=50; at $15, Qd=70 and Qs=70; at $20, Qd=50 and Qs=90. The equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: Equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: both are 70 units at a price of $15.

questions.question: A labor union’s central economic role is to:
options: Bargain collectively with employers over wages and working conditions
questions.answer: Bargain collectively with employers over wages and working conditions
questions.explanation: Unions represent workers in collective bargaining over compensation, hours, benefits, and workplace conditions.

questions.question: A student can work a four-hour shift for $60 or attend a free review session during the same time. If the student attends the review, the opportunity cost is:
options: The full cost of the course
Four hours plus $60, counted as separate monetary costs
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up; here that is the forgone wage.

questions.question: At a price of $12, quantity demanded is 70 and quantity supplied is 100. Which outcome follows?
options: A shortage of 30 with upward price pressure
A surplus of 30 with downward price pressure
questions.answer: A surplus of 30 with downward price pressure
questions.explanation: Supply exceeds demand by 100 − 70 = 30 units. Unsold output creates pressure for the market price to fall toward equilibrium.

questions.question: If the price of tea rises and coffee is a substitute, what happens to the market for coffee, all else equal?
options: There is only movement down the coffee demand curve
questions.explanation: A higher price for a substitute makes coffee relatively more attractive, increasing coffee demand at every price.

questions.question: A new production technology lowers firms' costs. In the affected market, the immediate curve change is:
options: Quantity supplied falls along an unchanged curve
questions.explanation: Lower production costs make firms willing to supply more at each price, shifting supply right.

questions.question: At a price of $9, quantity demanded is 120 and quantity supplied is 80. The market has:
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by 40 units, creating a shortage and upward pressure on price.

questions.question: Demand increases while supply decreases. Which equilibrium result is certain?
questions.explanation: Both shifts raise equilibrium price; their effects on equilibrium quantity move in opposite directions, so quantity is ambiguous.

questions.question: Using the midpoint method, price rises from $20 to $24 while quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80. The elasticity magnitude is closest to:
questions.explanation: The quantity change is 20/90 = 22.22% and the price change is 4/22 = 18.18%; 22.22/18.18 ≈ 1.22.

questions.question: If demand is elastic, a seller's price increase will usually:
questions.explanation: With elastic demand, quantity falls by a larger percentage than price rises, so total revenue decreases.

questions.question: Which good is most likely to have inelastic demand?
options: A specific brand of luxury sunglasses
A life-sustaining medicine with few substitutes
Restaurant meals in a city with many alternatives
questions.answer: A life-sustaining medicine with few substitutes
questions.explanation: Necessity and lack of substitutes make buyers less responsive to price changes.

questions.question: A consumer maximizes utility across two goods when the last dollar spent on each provides:
options: The same marginal utility per dollar
questions.answer: The same marginal utility per dollar
questions.explanation: If one good yields more marginal utility per dollar, spending can be reallocated toward it to raise total utility.

questions.question: A snack's marginal utilities are 24, 16, 8, and 2. This pattern illustrates:
questions.explanation: The marginal utilities fall from 24 to 16 to 8 to 2, so every additional snack adds less satisfaction than the one before it; that is diminishing marginal utility.

questions.question: A firm's total cost rises from $420 at 10 units to $465 at 11 units. The marginal cost of the 11th unit is:
questions.explanation: Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the one-unit output change: $465 − $420 = $45.

questions.question: Which cost must fall continuously as output rises in the short run?
options: Average variable cost at every output level
Marginal cost at every output level
questions.explanation: The same fixed cost is spread over more units, so average fixed cost falls as output increases.

questions.question: When marginal cost is below average total cost, producing the next unit causes average total cost to:
questions.explanation: When marginal cost is below the current average total cost, the next unit costs less than the average of earlier units and therefore pulls that average downward.

questions.question: Which market is closest to perfect competition?
options: A patented medicine sold by one firm
A market with many wheat farms selling a standardized crop
A market dominated by three aircraft makers
questions.answer: A market with many wheat farms selling a standardized crop
questions.explanation: Many sellers, a standardized product, and limited individual price power approximate perfect competition.

questions.question: A monopolistically competitive firm differs from a perfectly competitive firm because it:
options: Cannot enter or exit the market
questions.explanation: Product differentiation gives a monopolistically competitive firm some price-setting power despite many rivals.

questions.question: A legal patent can support monopoly power primarily because it:
options: Creates a barrier that temporarily limits entry by rivals
Requires every buyer to purchase the product
Makes the firm a price taker
Guarantees the firm will earn a profit
questions.answer: Creates a barrier that temporarily limits entry by rivals
questions.explanation: A patent grants a time-limited exclusive right that can block competing sellers from offering the protected invention; it does not guarantee demand or profit.

questions.question: In a competitive labor market, firms' demand for labor is derived from:
options: The value of workers' marginal product
questions.answer: The value of workers' marginal product
questions.explanation: Firms hire labor because worker output contributes revenue; the value of marginal product links output demand to labor demand.

questions.question: A binding minimum wage is set above equilibrium. The simplified competitive model predicts:
options: A labor surplus because labor supplied exceeds labor demanded
questions.answer: A labor surplus because labor supplied exceeds labor demanded
questions.explanation: At the higher wage, more workers seek jobs while firms demand fewer workers, creating excess labor supply.

questions.question: If more people enter a local labor market while firms’ labor demand is unchanged, the simplified competitive model predicts:
options: Labor supply shifts right, putting downward pressure on the equilibrium wage
Labor demand shifts right, raising the equilibrium wage
Labor supply shifts left, creating a worker shortage
No change because population cannot affect labor markets
questions.answer: Labor supply shifts right, putting downward pressure on the equilibrium wage
questions.explanation: More available workers increase labor supply at each wage. With labor demand unchanged, the new equilibrium has a lower wage and higher employment quantity in the simplified model.
